The Fabric of Everyday Life

Every Saturday at 6:30 a.m., long before the first customers arrive, the vendors of the Riverbend Market begin unloading their trucks. The market has operated on the same four-block stretch of Alder Street since 1948, and by most accounts it has never missed a week.

Roughly 140 stalls now fill the street, up from 85 a decade ago. According to the city's 2023 survey, the market draws about 12,000 visitors on a typical weekend and generates an estimated $4.2 million a year for the local economy (not counting nearby cafes and shops).

"People think we sell vegetables," said Maria Okafor, who has run a produce stand here for 27 years. "What we really sell is a reason to come downtown." Her best-selling item, she added, is still the two-dollar bag of mixed greens.

The numbers support her. Foot traffic on market days is 38% higher than on other Saturdays, and three-quarters of visitors told surveyors they also stopped somewhere else in the neighborhood. Dr. Alan Whitfield, an economist at the state university, calls this the "spillover effect."

Not everything is rosy. Stall fees rose from $35 to $50 per day in January, and several long-time vendors say the increase is hard to absorb. Parking remains the most common complaint: the nearest public garage has only 220 spaces, and it is usually full by 9:15 a.m.

The city council is weighing a proposal to close two additional blocks to cars between May 1 and October 31. Supporters argue the change would add room for 40 more stalls; opponents worry about deliveries and access for older residents.

For now, the routine continues. By noon the bread is gone, the flower buckets are half empty, and a brass band (five retired schoolteachers who call themselves the Second Wind) is playing near the fountain. By 2 p.m., the trucks are loaded again.

A public hearing on the street-closure plan is scheduled for Thursday, March 14, at 7 p.m. in Room 204 of City Hall. Written comments may be sent to the clerk's office until the end of the month.
